questions.rationale: You likely thought destructuring a key that isn't there is an error, like reading something that doesn't exist. It isn't: `a` is simply bound to undefined. Only destructuring null or undefined as the whole source throws, and a default would replace the undefined.

query.title: Destructuring assignment
query.explanation: Destructuring requires the source to be coercible to an object. `null` and `undefined` fail that check and throw a TypeError before any property is read. A missing property on a real object does not throw; it binds undefined. Optional chaining is a different operator and is not implied by a destructuring pattern.

questions.rationale: You may have thought destructuring null just gives undefined for `a`, like a missing property on a real object. But null can't be coerced to an object, so the TypeError is thrown before any property is read. Only real objects bind undefined.

questions.prompt: In an object literal, `{ name }` means `{ name: name }`.

query.title: Object literals
query.explanation: Shorthand property syntax uses the identifier both as the key and as the value expression. `{ name }` is the same object as `{ name: name }`, so `person.name` is "Ada". It does not create a key with the value undefined, and it is not a destructuring pattern: that same brace shape on the left of `=` would unpack instead of build.

questions.prompt: A computed property name evaluates its expression.

query.title: Object literals
query.explanation: Brackets around a property name evaluate the expression and use the result as the key. `key` holds "id", so the object is `{ id: 1 }`, not an object whose key is the identifier "key". The expression can be any value that converts to a property key, including string concatenation such as `["a" + "b"]`.

query.title: Loops and iteration
query.explanation: `for...of` pulls values from the iterable protocol. On an array, the loop variable is "a" and then "b", the elements, not the index strings "0" and "1". `for...in` is the loop that yields keys. A plain object is not iterable, so `for...of` on `{}` throws.

questions.rationale: You probably thought for...of hands you keys or indexes like "0" and "1". It doesn't: it pulls values from the iterable, so value is "a" and then "b". Yielding keys is what for...in does.

questions.prompt: `for...in` yields enumerable string keys, including inherited ones.

query.title: JavaScript · Easy
query.explanation:
for...in walks enumerable keys

`for...in` enumerates enumerable string keys on the object and continues up the prototype chain, so both "own" and "inherited" appear. It does not yield values, and it skips non-enumerable properties and symbol keys. `Object.keys` is the own-only list, so an inherited enumerable key shows up in `for...in` and not in `Object.keys`.

questions.rationale: You likely thought for...in only visits an object's own properties. It actually keeps walking up the prototype chain, so the enumerable inherited key "inherited" shows up along with "own". Only Object.keys limits the list to own keys.

questions.prompt: `for...in` on an array yields the indexes as strings.

query.title: JavaScript · Easy
query.explanation:
Array indexes in for...in are strings

Array indexes are property keys, and property keys that `for...in` visits are strings. The loop variable is "0" and then "1", not the numbers 0 and 1, and not the elements "a" and "b". `for...of` is what yields the elements. Other enumerable keys, including inherited ones, are visited too.

questions.rationale: Picking false suggests you expected for...in on an array to give the elements "a" and "b", or numeric indexes. It actually visits property keys, which are always strings: "0" and "1". Use for...of to get the elements.

questions.prompt: `JSON.stringify` omits object keys whose value is `undefined`.

query.title: JavaScript data serialization
query.explanation: JSON has no undefined value. When an object property is undefined, `JSON.stringify` leaves that key out, so the result is '{"a":1}'. The key is not serialized as null. An undefined element inside an array is handled differently: that slot becomes null rather than disappearing.

questions.rationale: You probably thought JSON.stringify keeps every key, writing undefined as "b":undefined or "b":null. JSON has no undefined value, so the key is dropped and the result is '{"a":1}'. Only undefined inside an array becomes null.

questions.prompt: `JSON.stringify` turns an array hole, or an `undefined` element, into `null`.

query.title: JSON serialization of JavaScript values
query.explanation: In an array, both an explicit undefined element and a hole are serialized as null, so the slot stays in the JSON text. That differs from object properties, where undefined keys are omitted entirely. The array does not shrink, and the element is not left as the token undefined, which is not valid JSON.

questions.rationale: You likely thought JSON.stringify keeps undefined or drops it, as it does for object properties. In arrays it can't skip the slot, and undefined isn't valid JSON, so [1, undefined, 3] becomes "[1,null,3]" and the length stays the same.

questions.prompt: `JSON.stringify` omits function-valued properties of an object.

query.title: JSON serialization in JavaScript
query.explanation: Functions are not JSON values. `JSON.stringify` drops a function-valued property of an object the same way it drops undefined, so `b` is absent and the result is '{"a":1}'. A function element of an array is not dropped: that slot becomes null. The function source is never written into the JSON.

questions.rationale: You likely thought JSON.stringify keeps methods, maybe writing out their source. Functions aren't JSON values, so a function-valued property is dropped. Here b is omitted and the result is '{"a":1}'. Only array slots holding functions become null.

questions.prompt: `JSON.parse` of a JSON string returns the value that string describes.

query.title: Data serialization
query.explanation: `JSON.parse` reads JSON text and returns the corresponding value: an object, array, string, number, boolean, or null. `JSON.parse('{"a":1}').a` is the number 1, not a leftover string. Invalid JSON throws a SyntaxError. The reviver argument can rewrite values, but the default call returns the parsed data.

questions.rationale: You may have thought JSON.parse leaves you with text or some wrapper rather than real data. It reads the JSON and returns the value it describes, so '{"a":1}' gives an object whose .a is the number 1, not a string. Invalid JSON throws a SyntaxError.

questions.prompt: An arrow function cannot be constructed with `new`.

query.title: JavaScript · Easy
query.syntax: new (() => {});  // TypeError
query.explanation:
Arrows are not constructors

Arrow functions do not have a `[[Construct]]` internal method and do not get a `prototype` property. Calling one with `new` throws a TypeError. A `function` declaration or expression can be constructed with `new`. The arrow still runs fine as an ordinary call.

questions.rationale: You likely thought arrow functions work like regular functions and can be used as constructors. They can't: arrows have no [[Construct]] method and no prototype, so new on one throws a TypeError, even though calling it normally works fine.

questions.prompt: An arrow function does not bind its own `arguments` object.

query.title: JavaScript · Easy
query.syntax:
const f = () => arguments;
// in a module, f() throws ReferenceError
query.explanation:
Arrows have no own arguments

An arrow function does not create an `arguments` binding for its own parameters. At the top of a module, `arguments` is unresolved, so calling that arrow throws a ReferenceError. Nested inside a traditional function, the arrow sees that outer `arguments` object lexically, which lists the outer function's arguments, not the arrow's.

questions.rationale: You likely thought an arrow function gets its own `arguments` object like a regular function. It doesn't: arrows create no `arguments` binding, so the name resolves lexically to an outer function's `arguments`, or throws a ReferenceError at module top level.

questions.prompt: A function declaration is hoisted within its scope.

query.title: Functions and scope
query.explanation: A function declaration is initialized for the whole of its scope before that scope starts running, so a call on an earlier line succeeds. In strict mode the scope is the enclosing block or function, and the name does not leak out of that block. A `const` function expression does not get this treatment: touching it early throws.

questions.rationale: You likely thought a function must run its definition line before it can be called, so calling it earlier would fail. Declarations are initialized for their whole scope before any code runs, so the early call works. Only a const function expression throws early.

questions.prompt: A function expression assigned to `const` is in the temporal dead zone before its line.

query.title: JavaScript · Easy
query.explanation:
A const function expression is not hoisted

The `const` binding is hoisted but uninitialized, so a call before the declaration line throws a ReferenceError. The function value does not exist until that line runs. This is not the TypeError you would get from `var expression = function () {}`, where the hoisted binding is undefined and you try to call it. A function declaration, by contrast, can be called earlier in the same scope.

questions.rationale: You likely thought a function expression assigned to const is hoisted like a function declaration, so the call works. Only the uninitialized const binding is hoisted; calling it before its line throws a ReferenceError (temporal dead zone).

questions.prompt: A default parameter is used for `undefined`, and not for `null`.

query.title: JavaScript · Easy
query.explanation:
Defaults trigger on undefined only

A default parameter initializer runs when the argument is undefined, including when the caller omits it. `f(undefined)` therefore returns 1. `null` is a passed value, so `f(null)` returns null and the default does not run. The same rule rejects the idea that every falsy argument, such as 0, is replaced.

questions.rationale: Choosing false suggests you think null also triggers the default, so f(null) would return 1. A default only runs when the argument is undefined or omitted. null is a real passed value, so f(null) returns null and the default is skipped.

questions.prompt: A default parameter may read an earlier parameter.

query.title: JavaScript function parameters
query.explanation: Default expressions are evaluated left to right in a scope where earlier parameters are already initialized. `f(4)` leaves `b` undefined, so the default reads `a` and returns 4. A default cannot read a later parameter: that binding is still in the temporal dead zone, and the initializer throws a ReferenceError if it runs.

questions.rationale: You probably thought each parameter can't see the others, so b = a would fail. But defaults run left to right with earlier parameters already initialized, so f(4) lets b's default read a and returns 4. Only later parameters are off limits.

questions.prompt: `switch` compares the discriminant with each `case` using `===`.

query.title: JavaScript · Easy
query.explanation:
switch uses strict equality

Each `case` label is compared with the discriminant using `===`. The number 1 does not match the string "1", so that branch is skipped. There is no `ToNumber` coercion the way `==` would apply. The comparison is not a truthiness test of the case label.

questions.rationale: Picking false suggests you thought switch matches cases loosely, or by truthiness, so 1 and "1" would be treated as the same. In fact each case is tested with ===, so the number 1 never matches the string "1" and no type coercion happens.

questions.prompt: `switch` falls through to the next case when `break` is omitted.

query.title: Control flow statements
query.explanation: Once a `case` matches, execution continues into the following cases until a `break`, a `return`, or the end of the switch. Matching `case 1` and omitting `break` also runs the body of `case 2`. Cases are not isolated blocks. A `break` is what stops that fall-through.

questions.rationale: You probably thought each case is its own isolated block that stops by itself. In JavaScript, once a case matches, execution runs on into the following cases until a break, a return, or the end of the switch. Omitting break is what causes fall-through.

query.title: Unary operators
query.explanation: The `void` operator evaluates its operand, discards that value, and returns undefined. `void 0` is undefined, and a side effect inside the operand still happens. It does not delete a binding, and it does not return 0. The operand expression runs; only its result is thrown away.

questions.prompt: `delete` returns `true` when it removes a configurable own property.

query.title: JavaScript object property operations
query.explanation: A property created by an ordinary assignment is configurable. `delete obj.a` removes that own property and returns true. In strict mode, deleting a non-configurable property throws a TypeError instead of returning false. `delete` also returns true when the property was already absent, so true alone does not prove a field was there.

questions.prompt: `delete` on an array index leaves a hole and does not change `length`.

query.title: Array element operations
query.explanation: `delete items[1]` removes the own property at that index and returns true, but `length` stays 3. The index is then a hole: `1 in items` is false, while a direct read of `items[1]` is undefined. `splice(1, 1)` is what would close the gap and set `length` to 2. `delete` does not reindex the tail.

questions.rationale: Choosing false suggests you thought delete on an array element would shift the rest down and shrink length to 2. It doesn't: it only removes the property, leaving a hole at index 1 while length stays 3. splice(1, 1) is what closes the gap.

questions.prompt: The `in` operator is `true` for an inherited property.

query.title: Object property checks
query.explanation: The `in` operator returns true when the property is found on the object or anywhere on its prototype chain. `toString` lives on `Object.prototype`, so `"toString" in {}` is true even though `{}` has no own properties. `Object.hasOwn({}, "toString")` is false. `in` is not a check of the property's value.

questions.rationale: You probably thought `in` only sees a object's own properties, and `{}` has none. But `in` also searches the prototype chain, and `toString` lives on `Object.prototype`, so it is found and the result is true. Only `Object.hasOwn` checks own properties.

query.title: Object property checks
query.explanation: `Object.hasOwn` returns true only for an own property, whether or not that property is enumerable. `"toString" in {}` is true because of the prototype, but `Object.hasOwn({}, "toString")` is false. It does not invoke an instance method named `hasOwnProperty`, so a shadowed `hasOwnProperty` on the object cannot change the result.

questions.rationale: Picking false suggests you thought hasOwn would find inherited toString, like the in operator does. It doesn't: hasOwn only checks own properties and skips the prototype chain, so Object.hasOwn({}, "toString") is false, which makes the statement true.

query.title: JavaScript · Easy
query.syntax: Object.keys(obj)  // ["visible"]
query.explanation:
Object.keys lists enumerable string keys

`Object.keys` returns an array of the object's own enumerable string keys. A non-enumerable property such as "hidden" is left out, and a symbol key is left out, so the list is `["visible"]`. `Object.getOwnPropertyNames` includes non-enumerable string keys, and `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols` lists symbol keys. Inherited enumerable names are omitted too.

questions.rationale: Choosing false suggests you think Object.keys lists every own property, including "hidden" and the symbol key. It only returns own enumerable string keys, so here the result is ["visible"]. Other methods cover the rest, like getOwnPropertyNames and getOwnPropertySymbols.

query.title: JavaScript Math utilities
query.explanation: With no arguments, `Math.max` returns `-Infinity`, the identity value for maximum, so adding it to a later comparison cannot raise the result. It does not throw, and it does not return 0 or undefined. `Math.min()` with no arguments is the opposite identity, `Infinity`.

questions.rationale: You probably expected an empty call to give 0, NaN, or an error, as if there were nothing to compare. But Math.max() returns -Infinity, the identity for maximum: any real number compared against it is larger, so it never raises the result.

query.title: JavaScript · Easy
query.explanation:
Math.max does not unpack an array

`Math.max` converts each argument with `ToNumber`. One array argument becomes `ToNumber([1, 2, 3])`, the array stringifies to "1,2,3", and that is NaN. Spreading passes three separate numbers, and the greatest is 3. An empty array is a different input: `Math.max([])` is 0, because an empty array converts to 0.

questions.rationale: You likely thought Math.max reads the numbers inside an array, so both calls give 3. It doesn't unpack arrays: the array is converted to "1,2,3", which becomes NaN. Only spreading passes three separate numbers, so only that call returns 3.

query.title: JavaScript · Easy
query.explanation:
Plus concatenates when either side is a string

If either operand of `+` is a string, both sides are converted to strings and concatenated. The number 1 becomes "1", so the result is the string "51", not the number 6. Subtraction does not have a string mode: `'5' - 1` is the number 4. Evaluation is left to right, so `1 + 1 + "5"` is "25".

questions.rationale: You likely thought + always adds numbers, so '5' + 1 gives the number 6. But when either operand of + is a string, the other is converted to a string too and they are concatenated, so the result is the string '51'.

query.title: JavaScript · Easy
query.explanation:
Minus always coerces to numbers

The `-` operator converts both operands with `ToNumber` and subtracts. `ToNumber("5")` is 5, so the result is the number 4, not the string "4" and not NaN. `+` is the operator that would have concatenated these operands into "51". A string that is not numeric, such as "5px", becomes NaN under subtraction.

questions.rationale: You likely treated '5' - 1 like '5' + 1, where a string operand changes the result's type, or assumed a string can't be subtracted. But - converts both operands with ToNumber, so '5' becomes 5 and the result is the number 4.

query.title: JavaScript · Easy
query.syntax: true + true  // 2
query.explanation:
Plus numeric-coerces booleans

Neither operand of `+` is a string, so both are converted with `ToNumber`. `ToNumber(true)` is 1, and `1 + 1` is the number 2, not the boolean true. `true + false` is 1 by the same rule. `Boolean` context is unrelated: this expression never asks whether the sum is truthy.

questions.prompt: Which function returns a copy of an array of numbers sorted from smallest to largest?

choices.rationale: You likely assumed sort() orders numbers by value by default. Without a comparator it converts elements to strings and compares them as text, so [10, 9, 1] becomes [1, 10, 9]. Pass (a, b) => a - b to sort numerically.

criterion.statement: Sorts every array of numbers into ascending numeric order.

query.title: Array methods
query.explanation: Without a comparator, `sort()` converts every element to a string and orders them by UTF-16 code units, so `[10, 9, 1]` becomes `[1, 10, 9]`. Pass `(a, b) => a - b` to sort numbers by value.

questions.prompt: Which function returns true only when its argument is the number 0?

choices.rationale: You likely thought == compares values without changing types, so only the number 0 matches. But == converts both sides to a common type first, so '', '0', and [] all coerce to 0 and make this return true for them too.

criterion.statement: Returns true for the number 0 and false for every other value.
criterion.evidence: Fails for input "": expected false, got true

query.title: Comparison operators
query.explanation: Loose equality converts both sides to a common type before comparing, so `'' == 0`, `'0' == 0`, and `[] == 0` are all true. Strict equality compares type and value with no conversion, which is what a check for one specific value needs.

questions.prompt: Both snippets count how many of 2,000 numbers are in an allowed collection of 10,000. Which is faster?

choices.rationale: You may think includes() and Set.has() cost about the same per lookup. But includes() is a linear scan that walks the array each call, while Set.has() is a hash lookup that takes roughly constant time, so 2,000 repeated lookups favor the Set.

criterion.statement: Faster median run time on the same input.
criterion.evidence: A: 0.6 ms, B: 3.1 ms median on Node 24.21.0

query.title: JavaScript · Easy
query.explanation:
Membership tests: Array.includes versus Set.has

`array.includes(x)` is a linear scan. A `Set` is a hash table, so `set.has(x)` takes about the same time however many items it holds. For repeated lookups, build the Set once.

questions.prompt: Both snippets double 2,000 numbers into a new array. Which is faster?

choices.text: reduce() that spreads the accumulator each step
choices.code:
const values = Array.from({ length: 2000 }, (_, i) => i);
const doubled = values.reduce((result, value) => [...result, value * 2], []);
choices.rationale: You may have thought reduce with a spread accumulator costs about the same as map. But [...result, x] allocates a new array and copies everything built so far on every step, about n*n/2 copies in total. map() writes each result once.

choices.code:
const values = Array.from({ length: 2000 }, (_, i) => i);
const doubled = values.map((value) => value * 2);

criterion.statement: Faster median run time on the same input.
criterion.evidence: A: 2.6 ms, B: 0.094 ms median on Node 24.21.0

query.title: JavaScript · Easy
query.explanation:
Spreading inside reduce() is quadratic

`[...result, value]` allocates a new array and copies all of `result` into it. Doing that once per element copies about n * n / 2 elements in total. `map()` writes each result once.
